confidence_why: Merlan 1983 describes, in a stress section she calls 'far from complete', a tendency to penultimate stress with variable root stress, but Baker 1999 (revised as Baker 2008), a book-length study of Ngalakgan word structure repeated in Baker 2005, finds initial primary stress in simple words, medial stress only on heavy syllables, and initial-or-penultimate variation in four-syllable roots, so the two first-hand accounts genuinely differ on placement and type but the fuller study is the clear guide.

sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title: Baker 2001 'Geminate dissimilation as prosody in Ngalakan', confirmed via Glottolog and the MITWPL catalogue as pp.29-58 of Pensalfini & Richards (eds.), Papers on Australian Languages (MIT Working Papers on Endangered and Less Familiar Languages 2) — print-only (MITWPL, USD 19.95; AIATSIS B P418.25/P1), no DOI, no open copy found; its content is the thesis Ch 4 geminate-alternation analysis (prosodically conditioned segmental alternation), so it is prosody but not a primary word-stress statement and is low priority given the open-access thesis. The thesis chapter itself (Ch 4) could not be downloaded today (USyd repository returned not reachable by automated download on every route); Ch 1/2/3/5/6 are already. Re-reading the held Baker 1999 Ch 2 p.20/p.36 and Ch 5 pp.191-194 gives the first-hand stress statement of record: initial trochaic stress with heterorganic-cluster weight sensitivity and weightless geminates/NC clusters — contradicting the catalog's 'lexical' coding based on Merlan 1983 §2.13 and superseding it as deciding source (reclassify already queued by the 2026-09-16 check). new_statements.quote: On the whole, Ngalakgan has a trochaic stress system. In simple, monomorphemic words, stress is initial. Most monomorphemic words are disyllabic or trisyllabic. [p.20] ... Monomorphemic roots in Ngalakgan almost always have some stress on the first syllable. In disyllabic and trisyllabic forms, initial stress is also primary. In quadrisyllabic words, the initial stress may be primary or secondary, but in either case it is associated with a pitch movement. In longer words, stress is initial also. [p.36]

new_statements.locator: Ch 2 'Root, Word and Compound Stress', §2.1 Simplex words, p.20; summary paragraph p.36; quantity-sensitivity in Ch 5 §5.1 pp.191-194
new_statements.reading: Word stress is initial (left-aligned trochaic feet), with quantity sensitivity: a non-initial syllable closed by a heterorganic cluster takes primary stress, whereas geminates and homorganic nasal+stop codas are weightless for stress; open-syllabled quadrisyllabic roots vary between initial and penultimate primary stress but always keep initial stress. That is a fixed/weight-sensitive initial system, not 'lexical' stress; the catalog's 'tendency.. to be penultimate' comes from Merlan 1983's self-described incomplete sketch and does not survive Baker's fuller description.

new_statements.quote: p.4: "In many Australian languages, stress rules appear to apply to every suffix independently, before they are subjected to word-level phrasing. We have these kinds of stress patterns in Ngalakgan and many other Australian languages, such as Warlpiri (Nash 1986), Diyari (Austin 1981), Western Desert (Goddard 1985). The general pattern in these languages is that stress is regularly alternating from the first syllable (examples from Ngalakgan; Baker 1999): (8) a. pólo 'old person' b. kámala 'sky' c. káɳamùru '"long-nose" native honeybee' d. káɹaŋkàŋaɳìni 'wallaby sp.'" p.5: "But morphological structure disturbs the regular stress alternation: (9) a. (ʈótoyʔ)-ki aunt-your b. (ʈòtoyʔ)-(kí-kkaʔ) aunt-your-LOC c. (ʈòtoyʔ)-ki-p(púlu) aunt-your-PL" p.13: "virtually every root begins in a foot (unless forced to move by a medial heavy syllable: Baker 1999 Ch 5)"

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 101010 (1 = a stressed syllable) = initial with alternation) and as the existing Baker 1999 statement (initial, trochaic, weight-sensitive). It adds the morpheme-as-stress-domain claim (each productive polysyllabic suffix is its own foot) and reiterates the heavy-syllable exception, so it refines the domain description while agreeing on the placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In simple roots stress is initial and alternates rhythmically from the first syllable (trochaic left-headed feet, e.g. pólo, kámala, káɳamùru, káɹaŋkàŋaɳìni). In morphologically complex words each productive morpheme is footed independently: polysyllabic suffixes and clitics always carry their own foot, monosyllabic ones are footed only if the surrounding material allows, so the alternation is disturbed by morpheme boundaries (p.5, generalisation (10), citing Baker 1999: 79). Every root begins in a foot unless a medial heavy syllable forces the foot to move (p.13, pointing to Baker 1999 Ch 5 for the weight condition).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating secondary stress on odd syllables of a root (grave accents in (8c-d): káɳamùru, káɹaŋkàŋaɳìni). In (9b-d) the root carries the grave (ʈòtoyʔ) and the suffix foot the acute (kí-kkaʔ, púlu), i.e. the root's stress becomes secondary once a footed suffix follows; the paper explicitly sets the primary/secondary distinction aside for its analysis ('I ignore here the distinction between primary and secondary stresses', p.5).
new_statements.exceptions: Medial heavy syllable can pull the foot off the root's first syllable (p.13, deferring to Baker 1999 Ch 5); monosyllabic suffixes/clitics are footed only contingently; French-style phrasal stress contrasted with Ngalakgan morpheme-level stress in table (27), p.11.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works use the spelling Ngalakgan for the same language (Glottolog ngal1293 'Ngalakan'); no dialect is distinguished. Baker 2004 draws its Ngalakgan data explicitly from Baker 1999.

tone_statements.quote: In monomorphemic forms the prosodic head, indicated by H* accent anchoring, may be on the left-most foot (as in examples above), or at least for some words, may optionally be on the right-most foot (61). In the right- headed forms, secondary stress is realised by an H* accent on the first foot, with upstep on the head accent that follows. But in left-headed words, there is no accent after the initial H*, and it is unclear how or whether secondary stress is phonetically realised (B. Baker, 2008, p. 83).

sources.quote: Ch 2 p.20: 'On the whole, Ngalakgan has a trochaic stress system. In simple, monomorphemic words, stress is initial.' Ch 5 p.191-192: 'Ngalakgan is however a quantity sensitive language ... In Ch 2 I showed that metrical stress in Ngalakgan is trochaic, and aligned to the left edge of words and WORD-level morphemes ... In trisyllabic roots, we find a consistent distinction between those with medial stress and those with initial stress. With a handful of exceptions, forms with medial stress have a medial closed syllable'. p.194: 'In these forms, the geminate does not attract stress.'
sources.note: Primary stress is initial (trochaic, left-aligned) in monomorphemic words; all open-syllabled di- and trisyllables are initial-stressed; the system is quantity-sensitive: a medial syllable closed by a heterorganic (bigestural) cluster takes stress (L'HL), while geminate and homorganic NC codas do not count as heavy (p.194 exx. (4)-(6), p.199-200); quadrisyllables vary initial ~ penultimate primary but always have initial stress (p.36). This contradicts the catalog's 'lexical' coding, which rests on Merlan 1983 §2.13 (a description its author calls 'far from complete').

tone.quote: In all three languages, the main form of prosodic prominence is pitch accent, which is anchored to stressed syllables. ... We will see that in the three languages under consideration, prominence is mostly limited to pitch, associated with phrasal accentuation. ... All these languages allocate stress as a mostly predicable edge-based phenomenon of Σ and ω constituents ... Instead, I mark pitch accent diacritically as v́ for all three languages (4). In Ngalakgan only, there is secondary and primary stress, realised as accentual upstep, which I annotate as (Cv̀Cv)(Cv́Cv). ... These accents are assigned by phrase structure
